reason: The sources provide over 15 corroborating facts across six independent websites documenting the station's construction, scale, operation, and planned 2030 deorbit.
story: In 1998, the launch of the Zarya module marked the birth of humanity's largest orbital outpost: the International Space Station. Built by fifteen nations and five space agencies, this football-field-sized megastructure has an internal pressurized volume comparable to a Boeing 747 and has hosted continuous human life since November 2000. Orbiting 250 miles above Earth, it circles the planet every 90 minutes. Yet low Earth orbit is an unforgiving environment. Decades of intense thermal cycles, atmospheric drag, and structural aging are taking their toll. While commercial ventures from Axiom Space and Russia's planned replacement station prepare to spin off, the ISS itself cannot remain in orbit indefinitely. Abandoning it would leave a 400-ton behemoth to tumble uncontrollably back to Earth. Instead, NASA plans to deorbit the station around 2030, using a dedicated U.S. Deorbit Vehicle to guide the blazing complex down into the remote South Pacific Ocean.
angle: Humanity's largest, most expensive space structure—the size of a football field with the interior volume of a Boeing 747—is slated to be intentionally steered into the ocean around 2030 by a dedicated deorbit spacecraft.

claims.claim: Construction of the International Space Station began in 1998 with the launch of its first piece.
The inaugural module launched for the space station was the Russian-built Zarya.
The space station program is operated through an international partnership of five space agencies.
The space station partnership represents fifteen participating countries.
The space station has been continuously occupied by humans since November 2000.
The space station is the largest human spacecraft or structure ever constructed in space.
The space station completes an orbit of Earth roughly every 90 to 93 minutes.
The station orbits Earth at an altitude of approximately 400 kilometers (250 miles).
The station spans approximately 109 meters end-to-end, comparable to an American football field.
The station has an internal pressurized volume of 1,005 cubic meters (35,491 cubic feet), comparable to a Boeing 747 airliner.
The station can accommodate up to eight visiting spacecraft docked simultaneously.
Cargo supply craft serving the station include SpaceX's Dragon, Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, and Russia's Progress.
The station's robotic Canadarm2 is used to move modules and assist spacewalking astronauts.
The space station flies at an orbital inclination of 51.6 degrees.
In January 2020, NASA awarded Axiom Space a contract to attach commercial modules to the ISS.
Russia's MLM Nauka laboratory module launched and docked to the station in 2021.
The Nauka module's cooling system suffered an external radiator leak in orbit.
The International Space Station is planned to close down operations around 2030.
NASA plans to deorbit the station using a dedicated vehicle designated the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle.
NASA Administrator Charles Bolden stated that any mission to Mars is likely to be a global effort.

disputed: Total station program cost: Wikipedia cites approximately $150 billion USD, whereas Space.com cites $100 billion. The script should cite a range or attribute with 'costing over $100 billion.'

Deorbit versus orbit raising: NASA and Planetary Society analyze boosting the ISS to a graveyard orbit as cost-prohibitive and impractical, while Wikipedia notes that proposals to park the station in a higher orbit have gained congressional interest. The script should present ocean deorbit as the agency baseline while noting alternative proposals have been debated.

Assembly flight tally: NASA states 42 total assembly flights (37 Space Shuttle, 5 Russian rockets), whereas Wikipedia mentions over 40 assembly flights with 36 Space Shuttle flights. The script should use the broader phrase 'over 40 assembly flights.'
